subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the ellipse if focus = (1, −1), e = 2/3 and directrix is x + y + 2 = 0.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.61 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 67. NOT on an SSP page — book p.49 lists SSP pages 57,58,59,60 for this chapter; page 61 carries no SSP banner. Printed appearances: AP 16,22 · TS 19. Book p.61 prints no margin mark tags for this focus-directrix style question, so the 1+1+1+1 split here is OURS, following the natural four stages of a focus-directrix derivation (set up the ratio, square and substitute, expand, simplify) — the same four-stage shape used across this chapter's derivation-style answers. This is the first of two focus-directrix questions in the chapter (67, 68); this one gives an axis-aligned final equation with an xy term of −4, unlike Q68's oblique case. Ellipse is an SAQ-ONLY unit on the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.5). No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE BLM on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 are the orchestrator's back-test stand-in).

insider_note: The focus-directrix definition SP = e·PM works for any ellipse, tilted or not — it does not need the ellipse to already be lined up with the coordinate axes, which is why the final equation here carries an xy term.

steps.label: Set up SP = e·PM
steps.margin_note: First mark. S is the given focus, and PM is the perpendicular distance from P to the given directrix.
steps.memory_tip: SP over PM equals e — that ratio IS the definition of an ellipse.
lines: Let P(x₁, y₁) be any point on the ellipse
steps.why: The focus-directrix property defines the ellipse directly: the distance from any point P to the focus, divided by its perpendicular distance to the directrix, is always the constant e.
common_mistakes: Using the point-to-line distance formula without the √2 denominator that comes from the coefficients of x and y in x + y + 2 = 0.
Writing PM as the distance to the focus instead of to the directrix line.

steps.label: Square and substitute coordinates
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Squaring removes both the square root and the absolute value.
steps.memory_tip: Squaring both sides is always the next move once a ratio has a square root in it.
steps.why: Squaring both sides of SP = e·PM clears the square root on the left and the absolute value on the right, turning the equation into pure algebra.
common_mistakes: Squaring e = 2/3 incorrectly, getting 4/3 instead of 4/9.
Forgetting to also square the 3 in the denominator on the left, which is what produces the factor of 9.

steps.label: Expand both sides
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Expand each squared bracket term by term before collecting.
steps.memory_tip: Expand fully before simplifying — combining terms too early causes sign errors.
steps.why: Expanding both squared expressions fully, term by term, is what makes the next simplification step reliable.
common_mistakes: Missing the cross term 2x₁y₁ when expanding (x₁+y₁+2)², since it is not a perfect square of a single variable.
Sign-slipping on (y₁+1)², which expands with +2y₁, not −2y₁.

steps.label: Simplify to the final equation
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Collect all terms on one side and combine like terms carefully.
steps.memory_tip: This equation will have an xy term — that is expected, because the focus and directrix are not aligned with the coordinate axes.
steps.why: Collecting the x₁², y₁², x₁y₁ and linear terms separately, on the same side of the equation, gives the final second-degree equation of the ellipse.
common_mistakes: Combining 9x₁² and 2x₁² on the left with the wrong sign, giving the wrong coefficient of x₁².
Dropping the xy term entirely, mistakenly expecting an axis-aligned ellipse.
